chapter_text:
CHAPTER 20 - GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT IN PLANTS

Introduction

A tiny seed buried in the soil can, over weeks and years, become a towering tree. How does a single fertilised egg give rise to roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits, each in the right place and at the right time? The answers lie in the twin processes of GROWTH and DEVELOPMENT. Growth is the permanent and irreversible increase in the size, mass and number of cells of an organism. Development is the sum total of all the orderly changes - growth PLUS differentiation - that a plant passes through during its life cycle, from a germinating seed to a mature, flowering, senescing plant. This chapter explains how plants grow, how cells specialise, how chemical messengers called plant hormones regulate every stage, and how plants sense and respond to day length, cold and other signals of their environment.

20.1 GROWTH, DIFFERENTIATION AND DEVELOPMENT

GROWTH is defined as an irreversible, permanent increase in size, volume or dry weight of a cell, organ or whole plant, accompanied by an increase in the amount of protoplasm. Unlike animals, plants show growth throughout their life because they retain regions of permanently dividing cells called MERISTEMS. A plant grows in length at the tips of roots and shoots (apical meristems - primary growth) and grows in thickness through lateral meristems such as the vascular cambium and cork cambium (secondary growth). Because meristems keep the capacity to divide indefinitely, plants show what is called OPEN or INDETERMINATE growth.

DIFFERENTIATION is the process by which cells derived from meristems change in structure and function to perform specific jobs - a meristematic cell may become a water-conducting tracheid, a food-conducting sieve tube, a protective epidermal cell or a photosynthetic mesophyll cell. During differentiation cells lose the ability to divide, develop thick or specialised walls, and often lose their living contents (as in xylem vessels). DEDIFFERENTIATION is the reverse: living differentiated cells that had lost the power to divide regain it and become meristematic again - for example, the formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from mature parenchyma, or the mass of dividing cells (callus) formed when a plant is wounded or grown in tissue culture. REDIFFERENTIATION is the process in which the cells produced by such re-formed meristems mature once more into permanent tissues. DEVELOPMENT is the broadest term - it covers all the changes an organism goes through in its life cycle: growth, differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation, maturation and senescence. Development is controlled both by INTRINSIC factors (genes and hormones) and by EXTRINSIC (environmental) factors such as light, temperature, water and nutrients. The same genes can express differently under different conditions, a property called PLASTICITY - for example, heterophylly, where a plant produces differently shaped leaves in air and under water.

20.2 PHASES OF GROWTH AND THE GROWTH CURVE

Growth in a root or shoot tip occurs in three successive regions or PHASES. (1) The PHASE OF CELL DIVISION (meristematic phase): the cells of the apical meristem and their immediate derivatives divide repeatedly by mitosis. These cells are small, thin-walled, rich in protoplasm and have large nuclei. (2) The PHASE OF CELL ELONGATION (enlargement): just behind the meristem the newly formed cells increase greatly in size, take up water into enlarging vacuoles, deposit new wall material and become vacuolated. This is the region responsible for the actual increase in length. (3) The PHASE OF CELL MATURATION (differentiation): further behind, the enlarged cells attain their final size and differentiate into specific mature tissues, developing their characteristic wall thickenings and losing protoplasm where required.

MEASUREMENT OF GROWTH: growth can be measured as an increase in length, area, volume, fresh weight, dry weight or cell number. A simple instrument called the AUXANOMETER records the increase in length of a shoot over time by magnifying the movement with a lever and pointer over a scale. GROWTH RATE is the increase per unit time. Absolute growth rate is the total increase measured per unit time, while relative growth rate (RGR) is the growth expressed per unit of existing material per unit time, allowing fair comparison between plants of different sizes.

THE GROWTH CURVE: when the size of a plant (or organ, or population of cells) is plotted against time, the result is a characteristic S-SHAPED or SIGMOID curve. It has three phases. (a) The LAG PHASE, at the start, when growth is slow as the plant prepares itself (cells divide slowly and metabolism gears up). (b) The LOG or EXPONENTIAL PHASE, when growth is rapid and the rate increases with time - cells divide and enlarge most quickly. (c) The STATIONARY PHASE (also called the phase of diminishing growth or the steady state), when growth slows and finally stops as limits of size, nutrients and ageing are reached. The whole S-shaped pattern is called a SIGMOID GROWTH CURVE and is typical of cells, organs and whole organisms; the steepest, middle part is the grand period of growth.

20.3 SEED GERMINATION

A seed is a resting, dormant embryo packaged with stored food and protected by a seed coat. GERMINATION is the process by which the dormant embryo resumes active growth and develops into a seedling. Three external CONDITIONS are essential for germination: adequate WATER, suitable TEMPERATURE and sufficient OXYGEN; light is required by some seeds and inhibits others. Water is absorbed by IMBIBITION, causing the seed to swell and the seed coat to rupture; imbibed water activates enzymes and mobilises stored food. Oxygen is needed for the aerobic respiration that supplies energy for growth. A favourable temperature (usually 25-30 degrees C for many crops) is required for enzyme activity.

EVENTS OF GERMINATION: after imbibition, enzymes (such as amylases, proteases and lipases) become active and digest the stored starch, protein and fat into soluble sugars, amino acids and fatty acids that are translocated to the growing embryo. The RADICLE (embryonic root) emerges first, grows downward into the soil (positive geotropism) and anchors the seedling. The PLUMULE (embryonic shoot) then grows upward. On the basis of the fate of the cotyledons, germination is of two types. In EPIGEAL germination the HYPOCOTYL (the region below the cotyledons) elongates and pushes the cotyledons ABOVE the soil, where they often become green and photosynthetic before withering; examples are bean, castor and onion. In HYPOGEAL germination the EPICOTYL (the region above the cotyledons) elongates while the cotyledons remain BELOW the soil surface; examples are pea, gram, maize and rice. In cereals such as maize the plumule is protected as it pushes up by a sheath called the COLEOPTILE. A germinating seedling that has not yet turned green depends entirely on the food stored in its cotyledons or endosperm until it establishes leaves and begins photosynthesis.

20.4 PLANT GROWTH REGULATORS (PHYTOHORMONES)

Plant growth and development are coordinated by small amounts of chemical substances called PLANT GROWTH REGULATORS, PHYTOHORMONES or simply plant hormones. A hormone is produced in one part of the plant, may act where it is made or be transported to another part, and controls growth responses in extremely low concentrations. There are five classical groups: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene. The first three are broadly GROWTH PROMOTERS; abscisic acid is a GROWTH INHIBITOR; ethylene has mixed effects and is a gas.

AUXINS: The first hormone to be discovered. Charles Darwin and his son Francis, studying the bending of grass coleoptiles towards light (PHOTOTROPISM), showed that the tip senses light and some influence passes downward to cause bending; F. W. Went later isolated this substance from oat coleoptile tips and named it AUXIN (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA, is the natural auxin). Auxin is produced at growing shoot tips and moves downward. Its effects include: promotion of cell elongation; control of PHOTOTROPISM (auxin accumulates on the shaded side, so that side elongates more and the shoot bends towards light) and GEOTROPISM; APICAL DOMINANCE, in which the growing shoot tip suppresses the growth of lateral (axillary) buds - removing the tip (as in pruning or pinching) releases the side buds and makes the plant bushy; promotion of rooting in stem cuttings; prevention of premature fruit and leaf drop; and induction of parthenocarpy (seedless fruits). Synthetic auxins such as NAA and 2,4-D are used as rooting hormones, to prevent pre-harvest fruit drop and, at high doses, as selective WEEDKILLERS that kill broad-leaved weeds.

GIBBERELLINS: discovered from the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which caused the 'foolish seedling' (bakanae) disease of rice in which plants grew abnormally tall and thin. Gibberellins (GA, of which GA3 is best known) cause dramatic STEM ELONGATION, especially in dwarf plants (a dwarf pea treated with GA grows as tall as a normal plant), promote BOLTING (rapid elongation of the stem before flowering) in rosette plants such as cabbage and beet, break seed and bud DORMANCY, promote SEED GERMINATION (in barley, GA from the embryo triggers the aleurone layer to make amylase that digests starch, a fact used in the malting/brewing industry), and can substitute for the cold or long-day requirement of some plants. They also increase fruit size (as in grapes).

CYTOKININS: discovered as substances (kinetin, and the natural zeatin from maize) that promote CELL DIVISION (cytokinesis). Cytokinins are synthesised mainly in root tips and developing seeds and fruits. They promote cell division, help in the formation of new leaves, chloroplasts and lateral shoots, break apical dominance (working antagonistically to auxin), and notably DELAY the AGEING (SENESCENCE) of leaves by mobilising nutrients towards them (the 'Richmond-Lang effect') - which is why cytokinins keep cut flowers and vegetables fresh. The relative ratio of auxin to cytokinin controls whether a tissue-culture callus forms roots or shoots.

ABSCISIC ACID (ABA): a general GROWTH INHIBITOR, often called the STRESS HORMONE because it accumulates when a plant faces water shortage, cold or other stress. ABA promotes the CLOSURE of STOMATA during water stress (reducing water loss by transpiration), induces and maintains SEED and BUD DORMANCY, inhibits growth and seed germination, and promotes senescence and abscission. It is antagonistic to gibberellins. Because it prepares plants to survive adverse conditions, ABA is also known as the stress or dormancy hormone.

ETHYLENE: a simple GASEOUS hormone. Ethylene promotes the RIPENING of fruits (a ripe apple releases ethylene that hastens the ripening of nearby fruit - 'one bad apple spoils the barrel'), triggers ABSCISSION (shedding) of leaves, flowers and fruits, breaks dormancy in some seeds and buds, promotes flowering in pineapple and mango, and causes the 'triple response' and epinasty. Ethephon, a compound that releases ethylene, is sprayed to hasten uniform fruit ripening and to promote female flowers.

20.5 PHOTOPERIODISM AND PHYTOCHROME

Many plants flower only at particular times of the year, showing that they can measure the length of day and night. PHOTOPERIODISM is the response of plants (especially flowering) to the relative lengths of day and night, that is, to the PHOTOPERIOD. On this basis plants are grouped into three types. SHORT-DAY PLANTS (SDP) flower only when the day length is SHORTER than a certain critical value (long nights) - examples are chrysanthemum, rice, soybean and tobacco. LONG-DAY PLANTS (LDP) flower only when the day length is LONGER than a critical value (short nights) - examples are wheat, spinach, radish and henbane. DAY-NEUTRAL PLANTS (DNP) flower irrespective of day length - examples are tomato, cotton, maize and cucumber. Careful experiments showed that it is actually the length of the continuous DARK period (night) that is critical: interrupting the long night of a short-day plant with a brief flash of light prevents it from flowering. The LEAVES perceive the photoperiodic stimulus, but the response (flowering) occurs at the shoot tip, showing that a flowering signal - a hypothetical hormone named FLORIGEN - is produced in the leaves and transported to the growing points. The light signal is detected by a blue-green pigment called PHYTOCHROME, which exists in two interconvertible forms: Pr, which absorbs RED light (about 660 nm), and Pfr, which absorbs FAR-RED light (about 730 nm). Red light converts Pr to Pfr; far-red light (and darkness) converts Pfr back to Pr. Pfr is the biologically active form and controls flowering, seed germination and many other light-dependent responses.

20.6 VERNALIZATION AND PLANT MOVEMENTS

VERNALIZATION is the promotion of flowering by a period of LOW TEMPERATURE (cold treatment). Some plants, especially certain biennials and winter varieties of cereals (such as winter wheat), will not flower unless the young plant or the moist germinating seed is exposed to a spell of cold (near 0-5 degrees C) for some weeks. Vernalization shortens the vegetative phase and allows the plant to flower earlier; it is used, for example, to allow winter wheat to be sown in spring. The cold is perceived by the shoot apex (dividing cells), and the effect can sometimes be substituted by gibberellin.

PLANT MOVEMENTS: although rooted in one place, plants show movements, chiefly of curvature. TROPIC MOVEMENTS (tropisms) are directional growth movements in response to an external stimulus coming from a particular direction; the direction of the movement is determined by the direction of the stimulus. PHOTOTROPISM is growth towards (shoots) or away from (roots) light; GEOTROPISM (gravitropism) is growth in response to gravity - roots grow towards it (positive), shoots away from it (negative); HYDROTROPISM is growth of roots towards water; THIGMOTROPISM is the growth response to touch, as when a tendril coils around a support. NASTIC MOVEMENTS, by contrast, are NON-DIRECTIONAL - their direction does not depend on the direction of the stimulus. Examples include the folding of the leaflets of the sensitive plant Mimosa pudica when touched (thigmonasty/seismonasty, caused by rapid loss of turgor in the pulvinus), and the opening and closing of flowers in response to light or temperature (photonasty). Tropic movements are growth movements and are usually slow and permanent; nastic movements are often rapid and reversible turgor movements.

SENESCENCE AND DORMANCY: SENESCENCE is the final phase of development - the ordered ageing and death of cells, organs (as in leaf fall in autumn) or the whole plant. It involves breakdown of chlorophyll and proteins and the withdrawal of useful materials to other parts before the organ is shed at an ABSCISSION zone. DORMANCY is a state of suspended growth and very low metabolism that helps a seed or bud survive unfavourable seasons; it is maintained by inhibitors such as abscisic acid and broken by favourable conditions, light, cold stratification or gibberellins.

SUMMARY

- Growth is an irreversible increase in size/mass with more protoplasm; plants show open, indeterminate growth because of meristems (apical for length, lateral for girth).
- Differentiation makes meristematic cells specialise; dedifferentiation restores dividing ability (callus, cork cambium); redifferentiation matures them again; development is the sum of all these changes.
- Growth passes through phases of cell division, cell elongation and cell maturation; growth is measured with an auxanometer and follows a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve with lag, log (exponential) and stationary phases.
- Seed germination needs water, oxygen and suitable temperature; imbibition and enzymes mobilise stored food; the radicle emerges first; germination is epigeal (cotyledons raised above soil, e.g. bean/castor) or hypogeal (cotyledons stay below, e.g. pea/maize).
- Five phytohormones: AUXIN (cell elongation, phototropism, apical dominance, rooting, weedkiller); GIBBERELLIN (stem elongation, bolting, breaks dormancy, seed germination/malting); CYTOKININ (cell division, delays senescence); ABSCISIC ACID (stress hormone: stomatal closure, dormancy, inhibits growth); ETHYLENE (gaseous: fruit ripening, abscission).
- Photoperiodism is the flowering response to day/night length: short-day, long-day and day-neutral plants; the dark period is critical; leaves perceive the signal and export florigen; phytochrome (Pr/Pfr, red/far-red) is the light receptor.
- Vernalization is the promotion of flowering by cold treatment; plant movements are tropic (directional, e.g. phototropism, geotropism, thigmotropism) or nastic (non-directional, e.g. Mimosa leaf folding).
- Senescence is programmed ageing and death; dormancy is suspended growth that helps survive bad seasons, maintained by ABA and broken by gibberellin, light or cold.

topics.name: Growth, Differentiation and Development
topics.description: Growth as an irreversible increase in size and protoplasm; meristems and open (indeterminate) growth; differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation; development as the sum of all changes in the life cycle, controlled by genes, hormones and environment.

topics.name: Phases and the Growth Curve
topics.description: The three phases of growth (cell division, cell elongation, cell maturation); measurement of growth with the auxanometer and relative growth rate; the sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve with lag, log (exponential) and stationary phases.

topics.name: Seed Germination
topics.description: Conditions for germination (water, oxygen, suitable temperature); imbibition and enzymatic mobilisation of stored food; emergence of the radicle and plumule; epigeal versus hypogeal germination and the role of the coleoptile.

topics.name: Plant Growth Regulators (Hormones)
topics.description: The five phytohormones - auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene - their discovery, sites of action and roles in cell elongation, apical dominance, stem elongation, cell division, dormancy, stress responses and fruit ripening, and their practical uses.

topics.name: Photoperiodism and Phytochrome
topics.description: Response of flowering to the relative length of day and night; short-day, long-day and day-neutral plants; the importance of the dark period; perception by leaves and the florigen concept; the red/far-red photoreceptor phytochrome (Pr and Pfr forms).

topics.name: Vernalization and Plant Movements
topics.description: Promotion of flowering by cold treatment (vernalization); tropic (directional) movements such as phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism and thigmotropism; nastic (non-directional) movements such as the folding of Mimosa leaves; senescence and dormancy.

learning_outcomes.description: Define growth, differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation and development, and explain why plants show open (indeterminate) growth through meristems.
Describe the three phases of growth (cell division, elongation, maturation), the measurement of growth, and interpret the sigmoid growth curve with its lag, log and stationary phases.
Explain the conditions and events of seed germination and distinguish between epigeal and hypogeal germination with examples.
Name the five groups of plant growth regulators and describe their discovery, sites of production and principal physiological roles.
Apply knowledge of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene to explain and predict plant responses and their practical agricultural and horticultural uses.
Explain photoperiodism, classify plants as short-day, long-day and day-neutral, describe the role of the dark period and leaves, and describe phytochrome (Pr/Pfr) and florigen.
Explain vernalization and describe tropic and nastic plant movements, together with senescence and dormancy.
Analyse and distinguish tropic from nastic movements and relate vernalization, dormancy and senescence to a plant's survival and development strategy.

chapter_summary.title: Growth and Development in Plants - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Biology (314) summary explains how plants grow and develop: growth and differentiation, the phases and sigmoid growth curve, seed germination, the five plant hormones, photoperiodism and phytochrome, vernalization, plant movements, senescence and dormancy.

sections.heading: Growth, differentiation and development
bullets: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size, volume or dry weight with more protoplasm.
Plants show open (indeterminate) growth because meristems keep dividing: apical for length, lateral (cambium) for girth.
Differentiation makes meristematic cells specialise; dedifferentiation restores dividing power (callus, cork cambium); redifferentiation matures them again.
Development is the sum of growth, differentiation and maturation, controlled by genes, hormones and environment (plasticity).

sections.heading: Phases of growth and the growth curve
bullets: A root/shoot tip has three phases: cell division (meristematic), cell elongation (enlargement) and cell maturation (differentiation).
Growth is measured as length, area, weight or cell number; an auxanometer records increase in length.
Plotting size against time gives a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve.
The curve has a lag phase (slow start), a log/exponential phase (rapid) and a stationary phase (growth stops).

sections.heading: Seed germination
bullets: Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature; some seeds also need light.
Imbibition swells the seed; enzymes digest stored starch, protein and fat into soluble food for the embryo.
The radicle emerges first and anchors the seedling; then the plumule grows up (protected by the coleoptile in cereals).
Epigeal: cotyledons raised above soil (bean, castor). Hypogeal: cotyledons stay below (pea, gram, maize).

sections.heading: Plant growth regulators (hormones)
bullets: Auxin (IAA): cell elongation, phototropism, apical dominance, rooting of cuttings; synthetic 2,4-D is a weedkiller.
Gibberellin: stem elongation, bolting, breaks dormancy, promotes seed germination (malting).
Cytokinin: promotes cell division and delays leaf senescence (keeps produce fresh).
Abscisic acid: stress hormone - closes stomata, causes dormancy, inhibits growth. Ethylene (a gas): fruit ripening and abscission.

sections.heading: Photoperiodism, phytochrome, vernalization and movements
bullets: Photoperiodism: flowering response to day/night length - short-day, long-day and day-neutral plants; the dark period is critical.
Leaves perceive the photoperiod and export a signal (florigen); phytochrome (Pr absorbs red, Pfr absorbs far-red) is the receptor, Pfr being active.
Vernalization is the promotion of flowering by a cold treatment; gibberellin can sometimes substitute.
Movements are tropic (directional: phototropism, geotropism, thigmotropism) or nastic (non-directional: Mimosa leaf folding).

key_takeaways: Growth is an irreversible increase in size and protoplasm; plants show open growth because of ever-dividing meristems.
Development = growth + differentiation (+ dedifferentiation and redifferentiation), controlled by genes, hormones and environment.
Growth passes through division, elongation and maturation, and follows a sigmoid curve with lag, log and stationary phases.
Germination needs water, oxygen and warmth; the radicle emerges first; germination is epigeal (cotyledons up) or hypogeal (cotyledons stay down).
The five hormones - auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin (promoters), abscisic acid (inhibitor) and ethylene (gas) - regulate every stage of the life cycle.
Photoperiodism (measured via the dark period, perceived by leaves, receptor phytochrome Pr/Pfr) and vernalization (cold) control the timing of flowering.
Plant movements are tropic (directional) or nastic (non-directional); senescence is programmed ageing and dormancy helps survival.

glossary.definition: A permanent, irreversible increase in the size, volume or dry weight of a cell, organ or plant, with an increase in protoplasm.
A region of permanently dividing cells; apical meristems increase length, lateral meristems (cambium) increase girth.
The process by which meristematic cells change in structure and function to become specialised mature cells.
The regaining of the power of division by mature, differentiated living cells, as in the formation of callus or cork cambium.
The S-shaped curve of size against time, with a lag phase, a log (exponential) phase and a stationary phase.
The process by which a dormant seed embryo resumes growth to form a seedling, needing water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.
Germination in which the hypocotyl raises the cotyledons above the soil, as in bean and castor.
Germination in which the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain below the soil, as in pea, gram and maize.
A plant hormone (IAA) causing cell elongation, phototropism and apical dominance; synthetic forms are used as rooting hormones and weedkillers.
A hormone causing stem elongation and bolting, breaking dormancy and promoting seed germination (as in malting).
A hormone that promotes cell division and delays the senescence (ageing) of leaves and cut produce.
The stress hormone; it closes stomata under water stress, induces dormancy and inhibits growth.
The response of plants, especially flowering, to the relative lengths of day and night (the photoperiod).
The pigment that perceives light for photoperiodism, existing as Pr (absorbs red) and active Pfr (absorbs far-red).
The promotion of flowering by exposing a plant or germinating seed to a period of low temperature (cold treatment).

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Growth and Development in Plants (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and to the point; give examples where asked. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Define growth and explain why plants are said to show open or indeterminate growth.
questions.answer: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in the size, volume or dry weight of a cell, organ or whole plant, accompanied by an increase in the amount of protoplasm. Plants show OPEN or INDETERMINATE growth because they retain regions of permanently dividing cells called meristems throughout their life. Apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots add length, while lateral meristems (cambium) add girth, so a plant can keep growing indefinitely, unlike animals whose growth stops at maturity.
questions.explanation: Definition + role of meristems for continuous growth.

questions.question: Distinguish between differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation.
questions.answer: Differentiation is the process by which cells derived from meristems change in structure and function to become specialised mature cells (e.g. tracheids, sieve tubes). Dedifferentiation is the reverse process, in which mature, differentiated living cells regain the power to divide and become meristematic again (e.g. formation of cork cambium or callus). Redifferentiation is the process in which the cells produced by such re-formed meristems again mature into specific permanent tissues, losing the power to divide.
questions.explanation: Three linked processes: specialise -> regain division -> mature again.

questions.question: Draw (describe) the sigmoid growth curve and name its three phases.
questions.answer: When the size of a plant or organ is plotted against time, an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve is obtained. It has three phases: (1) the LAG phase, at the beginning, where growth is slow as the plant prepares itself; (2) the LOG or EXPONENTIAL phase, the steep middle part, where growth is most rapid and the rate keeps increasing; and (3) the STATIONARY phase, where growth slows down and finally stops as limits of size, nutrients and ageing are reached.
questions.explanation: S-shaped curve: lag (slow), log (rapid), stationary (stops).

questions.question: State the three external conditions necessary for seed germination and give the role of each.
questions.answer: Water: absorbed by imbibition, it swells the seed, ruptures the seed coat, and activates enzymes that mobilise the stored food. Oxygen: needed for aerobic respiration, which releases the energy required for the growth of the embryo. Suitable temperature: needed for the activity of the enzymes that digest and translocate food; most crop seeds germinate best at about 25-30 degrees C. (Some seeds additionally require or are inhibited by light.)
questions.explanation: Water (imbibition/enzymes), oxygen (respiration), temperature (enzyme activity).

questions.question: Distinguish between epigeal and hypogeal germination with examples, and state the role of the coleoptile in cereals.
questions.answer: In EPIGEAL germination the hypocotyl (the part of the axis below the cotyledons) elongates rapidly and pushes the cotyledons ABOVE the soil surface, where they may turn green and photosynthesise before withering; examples are bean, castor and onion. In HYPOGEAL germination the epicotyl (the part above the cotyledons) elongates while the cotyledons remain BELOW the soil surface; examples are pea, gram, maize and rice. In cereals such as maize, the plumule (embryonic shoot) is protected as it is pushed up through the soil by a protective sheath called the COLEOPTILE, which prevents damage to the delicate shoot tip and, once above ground, splits to let the first leaves emerge.
questions.explanation: Epigeal = cotyledons raised (hypocotyl); hypogeal = cotyledons stay (epicotyl); coleoptile protects plumule.

questions.question: What is apical dominance? How can a gardener use this knowledge to make a plant bushy?
questions.answer: Apical dominance is the phenomenon in which the growing shoot tip (apical bud), through the auxin it produces, suppresses the growth of the lateral (axillary) buds below it. Because of this, the plant tends to grow tall rather than branch. A gardener can remove or pinch off the shoot tip (a practice called pruning or pinching); this removes the source of auxin, releases the lateral buds from suppression, and allows many side branches to grow, making the plant bushy and dense.
questions.explanation: Apical bud auxin suppresses side buds; removing the tip releases them.

questions.question: Name the five groups of plant hormones and state whether each is mainly a growth promoter or inhibitor.
questions.answer: The five groups are: (1) Auxins - growth promoters (cell elongation); (2) Gibberellins - growth promoters (stem elongation); (3) Cytokinins - growth promoters (cell division); (4) Abscisic acid (ABA) - a growth inhibitor (stress/dormancy hormone); and (5) Ethylene - a gaseous hormone with mixed effects, chiefly promoting fruit ripening and abscission.
questions.explanation: Auxin, GA, cytokinin (promoters); ABA (inhibitor); ethylene (gas, mixed).

questions.question: Why is abscisic acid called the stress hormone? Give two of its effects.
questions.answer: Abscisic acid (ABA) is called the stress hormone because its level rises sharply when a plant is under stress - such as drought, cold or salt - and it helps the plant survive these unfavourable conditions. Two of its effects are: (1) it causes the CLOSURE of stomata during water stress, reducing water loss by transpiration; and (2) it induces and maintains DORMANCY in seeds and buds, and inhibits growth and germination, so the plant remains inactive until conditions improve.
questions.explanation: Rises under stress; closes stomata; induces dormancy/inhibits growth.

questions.question: Explain photoperiodism. Classify plants on the basis of their photoperiodic response with one example each, and explain why the dark period is considered critical.
questions.answer: Photoperiodism is the response of plants, especially the induction of flowering, to the relative lengths of day and night (the photoperiod). On this basis plants are of three types. SHORT-DAY PLANTS (SDP) flower only when the day length is shorter than a critical value (i.e. long nights), e.g. chrysanthemum (also rice, soybean). LONG-DAY PLANTS (LDP) flower only when the day length is longer than a critical value (short nights), e.g. wheat (also spinach, radish). DAY-NEUTRAL PLANTS (DNP) flower irrespective of day length, e.g. tomato (also cotton, maize). Experiments show that it is really the length of the continuous DARK period that matters: if the long night of a short-day plant is interrupted by even a brief flash of light, the plant fails to flower, whereas interrupting the day makes no difference. Hence the uninterrupted dark period is the critical factor controlling flowering. The photoperiod is perceived by the leaves, which then export a flowering signal (florigen) to the shoot tips.
questions.explanation: Definition; SDP/LDP/DNP with examples; night-break experiment shows dark period is critical.

questions.question: What is vernalization? Distinguish briefly between tropic and nastic movements with one example each.
questions.answer: Vernalization is the promotion of flowering by exposing a plant or its germinating seed to a period of low temperature (cold treatment), as in winter wheat, which will not flower unless chilled. TROPIC movements are directional growth movements whose direction is determined by the direction of the stimulus - for example phototropism, the bending of a shoot towards light. NASTIC movements are non-directional movements whose direction does not depend on the direction of the stimulus - for example the rapid folding of the leaflets of Mimosa pudica (the sensitive plant) when touched, caused by loss of turgor.
questions.explanation: Vernalization = cold-induced flowering; tropic = directional (phototropism); nastic = non-directional (Mimosa).

questions.question: What is a meristem? Name its two main types by position.
questions.answer: A meristem is a region of permanently dividing cells that adds new cells to the plant body. The two main types by position are apical meristems (at the tips of roots and shoots, adding length) and lateral meristems (such as the vascular and cork cambium, adding girth). Intercalary meristems occur at the base of internodes/leaves.
questions.explanation: Meristem = dividing cells; apical (length) and lateral (girth).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by dedifferentiation and give one example.
questions.answer: Dedifferentiation is the process in which mature, differentiated living cells that had lost the power of division regain it and become meristematic again. For example, fully mature parenchyma cells in a stem may dedifferentiate to form the interfascicular cambium or the cork cambium (phellogen); similarly, wounded tissue or an explant in culture forms a dividing mass called callus.
questions.explanation: Mature cells regain division; e.g. cork cambium/callus.

questions.question: Differentiate between growth and development.
questions.answer: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in the size, mass or dry weight of a cell, organ or plant. Development is a broader term - it is the sum total of all the orderly changes that a plant passes through during its life cycle, including growth, differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation, maturation and senescence. Thus growth is one component of development.
questions.explanation: Growth = size increase; development = all life-cycle changes.

questions.question: Name and describe the phase of growth responsible for increase in length.
questions.answer: The phase of cell elongation (enlargement) is responsible for increase in length. Just behind the meristem, the newly formed cells greatly increase in size by taking up water into enlarging vacuoles and depositing new wall material, so the root or shoot lengthens.
questions.explanation: Cell elongation phase increases length via vacuolation.

questions.question: Describe the three phases of the sigmoid growth curve.
questions.answer: The sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve has three phases. In the LAG phase growth is slow as the plant prepares and metabolism gears up. In the LOG (exponential) phase growth is very rapid and the rate increases with time as cells divide and enlarge fastest. In the STATIONARY phase growth slows and finally stops as limits of size, nutrients and ageing set in.
questions.explanation: Lag (slow), log (rapid), stationary (stops).

questions.question: How would you measure the growth in length of a shoot in the laboratory?
questions.answer: Growth in length can be measured with an auxanometer. A thread is attached to the shoot tip and passes over a pulley carrying a pointer that moves over a scale; as the shoot grows, the pointer magnifies and records the increase in length over time. Growth can also be estimated simply by measuring length with a scale at regular intervals.
questions.explanation: Auxanometer magnifies and records length increase over time.

questions.question: Distinguish between absolute and relative growth rate.
questions.answer: Absolute growth rate is the total increase in size (or weight) measured per unit time. Relative growth rate (RGR) is the growth expressed per unit of the existing material per unit time. RGR allows a fair comparison of growth between plants or organs of different initial sizes.
questions.explanation: Absolute = total per time; relative = per unit existing material per time.

questions.question: List the events that follow imbibition during seed germination.
questions.answer: After imbibition of water, the seed swells and the seed coat ruptures. Enzymes such as amylase, protease and lipase become active and digest the stored starch, protein and fat into soluble sugars, amino acids and fatty acids, which are translocated to the growing embryo. The radicle then emerges, followed by the plumule, forming the seedling.
questions.explanation: Imbibition -> enzymes -> food mobilised -> radicle then plumule.

questions.question: Compare epigeal and hypogeal germination with one example each.
questions.answer: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and pushes the cotyledons above the soil, where they may become green (e.g. bean, castor). In hypogeal germination the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons remain below the soil surface (e.g. pea, maize). The key difference is whether the cotyledons are raised above the ground or stay buried.
questions.explanation: Epigeal (hypocotyl, cotyledons up, bean) vs hypogeal (epicotyl, cotyledons down, pea).

questions.question: Why does the radicle emerge before the plumule during germination?
questions.answer: The radicle (embryonic root) emerges first so that it can grow downward into the soil (positive geotropism), anchor the young seedling and start absorbing water and minerals. This support and water supply are needed before the plumule grows upward and the seedling begins to photosynthesise.
questions.explanation: Radicle first to anchor and absorb water before the shoot grows.

questions.question: Name the five plant hormones and state one function of each.
questions.answer: Auxin - promotes cell elongation and apical dominance; Gibberellin - causes stem elongation and breaks dormancy; Cytokinin - promotes cell division and delays senescence; Abscisic acid - closes stomata and induces dormancy (stress hormone); Ethylene - promotes fruit ripening and abscission.
questions.explanation: One role each: auxin, GA, cytokinin, ABA, ethylene.

questions.question: Describe the experiments of Darwin and Went that led to the discovery of auxin.
questions.answer: Charles Darwin and his son Francis observed that grass coleoptiles bend towards light (phototropism) and showed that the TIP perceives the light while the bending occurs lower down, so some influence must pass downward from the tip. Later, F. W. Went placed cut coleoptile tips on agar blocks, then put the blocks on decapitated coleoptiles; the coleoptiles bent, proving a chemical had diffused into the agar. Went named this growth-promoting chemical auxin.
questions.explanation: Darwin: tip senses light, influence moves down; Went: agar-block isolation of auxin.

questions.question: State two functions of gibberellins.
questions.answer: Gibberellins cause marked stem elongation, especially in dwarf plants, and induce bolting in rosette plants. They also break seed and bud dormancy and promote seed germination (e.g. by triggering amylase in barley during malting). (Any two.)
questions.explanation: Stem elongation/bolting; breaking dormancy/germination.

questions.question: How do cytokinins delay senescence, and why is this useful?
questions.answer: Cytokinins delay the ageing (senescence) of leaves by mobilising nutrients towards the treated tissue and slowing the breakdown of chlorophyll and proteins (the Richmond-Lang effect). This is useful in keeping cut flowers, leafy vegetables and fruits fresh and green for longer during storage and transport.
questions.explanation: Cytokinin slows chlorophyll/protein loss; keeps produce fresh.

questions.question: List three effects of ethylene on plants.
questions.answer: Ethylene promotes the ripening of fruits, triggers the abscission (shedding) of leaves, flowers and fruits, and promotes flowering in plants such as pineapple and mango. It also breaks dormancy in some seeds and buds. (Any three.)
questions.explanation: Fruit ripening, abscission, flowering in pineapple/mango.

questions.question: A farmer wants seedless grapes of larger size and to prevent apples dropping before harvest. Which hormones would you suggest and why?
questions.answer: For larger, seedless grapes, gibberellin (GA) is sprayed - it increases fruit size and can promote parthenocarpy (seedless fruit). To prevent premature dropping of apples before harvest, an auxin spray (such as NAA) is used, because auxin prevents the formation of the abscission layer and so stops fruit drop until the crop is ready.
questions.explanation: GA for large seedless grapes; auxin to prevent pre-harvest drop.

questions.question: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light.
questions.answer: When light falls on one side of a shoot tip, auxin moves to and accumulates on the SHADED side. The extra auxin there makes the cells on the shaded side elongate more than those on the lit side. This unequal elongation curves the shoot so that it bends towards the light - the response called positive phototropism.
questions.explanation: Auxin gathers on shaded side; more elongation there bends shoot to light.

questions.question: Auxin promotes growth of the shoot but the same concentration may inhibit roots. What does this tell you about hormone action?
questions.answer: It shows that the effect of a plant hormone depends on the tissue and on the concentration, not just on the hormone itself. A concentration of auxin that is optimal (promotes elongation) for shoots may be too high (supra-optimal) and therefore inhibitory for roots, which respond to much lower auxin levels. Thus the same hormone can promote or inhibit growth depending on concentration and the responding organ - hormone action is concentration- and tissue-dependent.
questions.explanation: Same hormone, different effect by concentration and tissue sensitivity.

questions.question: What is photoperiodism? Name the three categories of plants based on it.
questions.answer: Photoperiodism is the response of plants, especially the induction of flowering, to the relative lengths of day and night (the photoperiod). Based on it, plants are of three types: short-day plants (flower when day length is below a critical value), long-day plants (flower when day length is above a critical value) and day-neutral plants (flower irrespective of day length).
questions.explanation: Response to day/night length; SDP, LDP, DNP.

questions.question: Describe the two forms of phytochrome and how they interconvert.
questions.answer: Phytochrome exists in two interconvertible forms. Pr absorbs RED light (about 660 nm) and Pfr absorbs FAR-RED light (about 730 nm). Red light converts Pr to Pfr, while far-red light (and darkness) converts Pfr back to Pr. Pfr is the biologically active form controlling flowering and other responses.
questions.explanation: Pr (red) <-> Pfr (far-red); Pfr active.

questions.question: What is vernalization and why is it agriculturally useful?
questions.answer: Vernalization is the promotion of flowering by exposing a plant or its germinating seed to a period of low temperature (cold treatment). It is agriculturally useful because it shortens the vegetative phase and lets a crop flower earlier; for example, winter varieties of wheat can be vernalized and then sown in spring, allowing them to flower and be harvested in the same season.
questions.explanation: Cold-induced flowering; lets winter crops flower earlier.

questions.question: What is dormancy and how is it beneficial to a plant?
questions.answer: Dormancy is a state of suspended growth and very low metabolism in seeds or buds. It is beneficial because it lets the plant survive unfavourable seasons (cold winter or dry period) in a resting state, and ensures that germination or growth resumes only when conditions become favourable, improving the chance of survival.
questions.explanation: Suspended growth to survive bad seasons; resumes when favourable.

questions.question: Explain the terms growth, differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation and development, and how they are related.
questions.answer: GROWTH is a permanent, irreversible increase in size, volume or dry weight of a cell, organ or plant, with an increase in protoplasm; it occurs at meristems. DIFFERENTIATION is the process by which cells produced by meristems change in structure and function to become specialised mature cells (e.g. tracheids, sieve tubes, fibres), often losing the power to divide. DEDIFFERENTIATION is the reverse: mature, differentiated living cells regain the capacity to divide and become meristematic again, as in the formation of interfascicular cambium, cork cambium or callus. REDIFFERENTIATION is the maturation of the cells produced by these re-formed meristems into permanent tissues once more. DEVELOPMENT is the broadest term - the sum total of all the orderly changes an organism undergoes in its life cycle, i.e. growth plus differentiation (and de-/redifferentiation), maturation and senescence, controlled by both genes/hormones (intrinsic) and the environment (extrinsic).
questions.explanation: Definitions and the chain: growth -> differentiation -> de/redifferentiation, all part of development.

questions.question: Describe the phases of growth in a root tip and explain the sigmoid growth curve.
questions.answer: A growing root (or shoot) tip has three successive regions or phases. (1) PHASE OF CELL DIVISION: cells of the apical meristem divide repeatedly; they are small, thin-walled and rich in protoplasm. (2) PHASE OF CELL ELONGATION: just behind the meristem the new cells enlarge greatly, taking up water into vacuoles and adding wall material; this region actually increases the length. (3) PHASE OF CELL MATURATION: further back, the enlarged cells differentiate into specific mature tissues. If the total size is plotted against time, an S-shaped SIGMOID curve results, with a LAG phase (slow initial growth), a LOG or EXPONENTIAL phase (rapid growth, the grand period), and a STATIONARY phase (growth slows and stops). This pattern is typical of individual cells, organs and whole organisms.
questions.explanation: Division, elongation, maturation; sigmoid curve with lag, log, stationary phases.

questions.question: Describe the conditions and events of seed germination, and distinguish epigeal from hypogeal germination.
questions.answer: CONDITIONS: germination requires adequate water, sufficient oxygen and a suitable temperature (light is needed by some seeds). EVENTS: water is taken up by imbibition, swelling the seed and rupturing the coat; enzymes (amylase, protease, lipase) become active and digest stored starch, protein and fat into soluble sugars, amino acids and fatty acids that move to the embryo; oxygen supports the respiration that provides energy. The radicle emerges first and grows down to anchor and absorb water; the plumule then grows up. EPIGEAL vs HYPOGEAL: in epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above the soil (bean, castor); in hypogeal germination the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons stay below the soil (pea, maize). In cereals the coleoptile protects the emerging plumule.
questions.explanation: Conditions (water/O2/temperature), events (imbibition, enzymes, radicle then plumule), epigeal vs hypogeal.

questions.question: Give an account of the five groups of plant growth regulators, mentioning one discovery detail and the main roles of each.
questions.answer: AUXIN (IAA): discovered through Darwin's phototropism studies and Went's coleoptile-tip experiments; it promotes cell elongation, controls phototropism and geotropism, maintains apical dominance, promotes rooting and prevents fruit/leaf drop. GIBBERELLIN (GA): isolated from the fungus Gibberella (bakanae disease of rice); it causes stem elongation, bolting, breaks dormancy and promotes seed germination (malting). CYTOKININ: discovered as kinetin/zeatin; formed in root tips and seeds, it promotes cell division, forms new organs and delays leaf senescence. ABSCISIC ACID (ABA): the stress hormone; it closes stomata under water stress, induces seed and bud dormancy and inhibits growth. ETHYLENE: a gaseous hormone; it promotes fruit ripening, abscission of leaves and fruits, and flowering in pineapple. The first three are promoters, ABA is an inhibitor, and ethylene has mixed effects.
questions.explanation: Discovery + main roles of auxin, GA, cytokinin, ABA, ethylene.

questions.question: Discuss the practical (agricultural and horticultural) uses of plant hormones with examples.
questions.answer: Plant hormones have many practical uses. AUXINS: synthetic auxins (NAA, IBA) are rooting hormones for stem cuttings; auxins prevent pre-harvest fruit drop and induce seedless (parthenocarpic) fruits; 2,4-D at high dose is a selective weedkiller of broad-leaved weeds. GIBBERELLINS: used to increase the size of grapes, to speed and standardise malting of barley (amylase production), to induce bolting for seed production, and to break dormancy. CYTOKININS: used to keep cut flowers and leafy vegetables fresh by delaying senescence, and in tissue culture (with auxin) to control shoot/root formation. ABSCISIC ACID: helps plants tolerate drought by closing stomata and is linked to storing seeds in dormancy. ETHYLENE (as ethephon): hastens uniform ripening of fruits like tomato, mango and banana, promotes flowering in pineapple, and encourages female flowers in cucurbits. Thus hormones are widely used to control rooting, flowering, fruiting, ripening, dormancy and weeds.
questions.explanation: Uses of auxin, GA, cytokinin, ABA and ethylene with examples.

questions.question: Explain photoperiodism, the role of the dark period and the leaves, and the part played by phytochrome and florigen in flowering.
questions.answer: PHOTOPERIODISM is the response of flowering to the relative lengths of day and night. Short-day plants (e.g. chrysanthemum) flower when the day is shorter than a critical length; long-day plants (e.g. wheat) flower when it is longer; day-neutral plants (e.g. tomato) flower regardless. The DARK PERIOD is critical: interrupting the long night of a short-day plant with a flash of light stops flowering, showing that the continuous night length, not the day length, is measured. The LEAVES perceive the photoperiodic stimulus and produce a flowering signal - the hypothetical hormone FLORIGEN - which is transported to the shoot tips where flowers form. The light is detected by the pigment PHYTOCHROME, which exists as Pr (absorbs red, 660 nm) and Pfr (absorbs far-red, 730 nm); red light forms Pfr, far-red and darkness re-form Pr, and Pfr is the active form that regulates flowering.
questions.explanation: Definition; SDP/LDP/DNP; dark period critical; leaves + florigen; phytochrome Pr/Pfr.

questions.question: Describe the different types of plant movements with examples, and explain senescence and dormancy.
questions.answer: Plant movements are chiefly of curvature and are of two kinds. TROPIC movements (tropisms) are directional growth movements whose direction is set by the direction of the stimulus: phototropism (shoots grow towards light), geotropism/gravitropism (roots towards gravity, shoots away), hydrotropism (roots towards water) and thigmotropism (tendrils coil around a support on touch). NASTIC movements are non-directional and independent of the direction of the stimulus, such as the folding of Mimosa pudica leaflets on touch (seismonasty, from turgor loss in the pulvinus) and the opening/closing of flowers with light or temperature (photonasty). SENESCENCE is the programmed ageing and death of cells, organs (leaf fall) or the whole plant, involving breakdown and withdrawal of useful materials before shedding at an abscission zone. DORMANCY is a state of suspended growth and low metabolism (in seeds or buds) that helps the plant survive unfavourable seasons; it is maintained by inhibitors such as ABA and broken by light, cold or gibberellin.
questions.explanation: Tropic vs nastic movements with examples; senescence (ageing) and dormancy (rest).

questions.question: Analyse the differences between tropic and nastic movements and explain why both are useful to a rooted plant.
questions.answer: TROPIC movements are DIRECTIONAL: the direction of the response is determined by the direction of the stimulus, they are growth movements (permanent and usually slow), and they are curvature responses to stimuli such as light (phototropism), gravity (geotropism), water (hydrotropism) and touch (thigmotropism). NASTIC movements are NON-DIRECTIONAL: their direction is independent of the direction of the stimulus, they are often rapid and reversible turgor movements (not growth), e.g. the folding of Mimosa leaflets or the opening of flowers. Both are useful to a rooted, immobile plant: tropic movements let it position its organs advantageously - shoots grow into the light for photosynthesis, roots grow down and towards water for anchorage and absorption, and tendrils grip supports for climbing. Nastic movements give quick protective or adaptive responses - Mimosa folds its leaves to deter grazing, and flowers open and close with day/night to protect pollen and attract pollinators at the right time. Thus, although fixed in place, a plant can still respond effectively to its environment.
questions.explanation: Directional/growth (tropic) vs non-directional/turgor (nastic); each aids a fixed plant.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A gardener takes a healthy stem and grows a piece of it on a nutrient medium in the laboratory. First a mass of unspecialised dividing cells appears, and later, with the right balance of hormones, roots and shoots form from this mass.
(a) What is the mass of unspecialised dividing cells called?
(b) Which process forms it from mature stem cells?
(c) Name the process by which the mass later forms roots and shoots.
(d) Why can this be done in plants but not easily in adult animals?
questions.answer:
(a) The mass of unspecialised dividing cells is called a CALLUS.
(b) It forms by DEDIFFERENTIATION - mature, differentiated stem cells regain the power to divide.
(c) The callus later forms roots and shoots by REDIFFERENTIATION (differentiation into new organs).
(d) Many mature plant cells are TOTIPOTENT - they retain the ability to dedifferentiate and regenerate a whole plant, whereas most differentiated animal cells cannot do so, so tissue culture/regeneration is much easier in plants.
questions.explanation: Callus; dedifferentiation; redifferentiation; plant cell totipotency.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student measures the height of a bean seedling every two days and plots height against time. The graph rises slowly at first, then steeply, and finally levels off.
(a) What is the shape of this curve called?
(b) Name the three phases seen on it.
(c) In which phase is growth fastest?
(d) Which instrument could give a more precise record of length increase?
questions.answer:
(a) The curve is S-shaped, called a SIGMOID growth curve.
(b) The three phases are the LAG phase (slow start), the LOG or EXPONENTIAL phase (steep, rapid growth) and the STATIONARY phase (growth levels off).
(c) Growth is fastest in the LOG (exponential) phase - the grand period of growth.
(d) An AUXANOMETER, which magnifies and records the increase in length over time, gives a more precise record.
questions.explanation: Sigmoid curve; lag/log/stationary; fastest in log; auxanometer.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A bean seed and a pea seed are sown. In the bean, the cotyledons are carried above the soil and turn green; in the pea, the cotyledons remain below the soil while the shoot grows up.
(a) Name the type of germination in the bean and in the pea.
(b) Which region elongates in each case?
(c) Which organ emerges first in both?
(d) State one condition, besides water, that both seeds need to germinate.
questions.answer:
(a) The bean shows EPIGEAL germination; the pea shows HYPOGEAL germination.
(b) In the bean the HYPOCOTYL elongates (raising the cotyledons); in the pea the EPICOTYL elongates (cotyledons stay below).
(c) The RADICLE (embryonic root) emerges first in both.
(d) Besides water, both need OXYGEN (for respiration) and a suitable TEMPERATURE. (Any one.)
questions.explanation: Epigeal (bean, hypocotyl) vs hypogeal (pea, epicotyl); radicle first; oxygen/temperature.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A fungus infecting rice caused the plants to grow abnormally tall and thin, a condition called the 'foolish seedling' disease. Scientists later isolated the responsible chemical from the fungus.
(a) Which group of plant hormones was discovered this way?
(b) Name the fungus involved.
(c) State one effect of this hormone on dwarf plants.
(d) Give one industrial use of this hormone.
questions.answer:
(a) The GIBBERELLINS were discovered this way.
(b) The fungus involved is Gibberella fujikuroi.
(c) In genetically dwarf plants gibberellin causes stem ELONGATION, so a dwarf pea treated with GA grows as tall as a normal plant.
(d) Industrial use: gibberellin speeds the malting of barley (it triggers amylase to digest starch), used in the brewing industry; it is also used to increase the size of grapes. (Any one.)
questions.explanation: Gibberellin; Gibberella; elongates dwarfs; malting/grape size.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A gardener has three problems: (i) a tall, spindly plant that will not branch, (ii) cut flowers that wilt too quickly, and (iii) a field of broad-leaved weeds among the crop.
(a) How can the gardener make the plant bushy, and why does it work?
(b) Which hormone keeps the cut flowers fresh?
(c) Which chemical will selectively kill the weeds?
(d) Name the auxin effect responsible for problem (i).
questions.answer:
(a) The gardener should pinch/remove the shoot tips; this removes the source of auxin and releases the lateral buds from apical dominance, so side branches grow and the plant becomes bushy.
(b) CYTOKININ keeps cut flowers fresh by delaying senescence.
(c) The synthetic auxin 2,4-D will selectively kill broad-leaved weeds.
(d) Problem (i) is due to APICAL DOMINANCE, the suppression of lateral buds by auxin from the shoot tip.
questions.explanation: Pinch tip (breaks apical dominance); cytokinin; 2,4-D; apical dominance.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A fruit seller keeps unripe mangoes in a closed box with a few ripe apples, and finds that the mangoes ripen quickly. Bananas kept beside ripe fruit also ripen faster.
(a) Which gaseous hormone released by the ripe fruit causes this?
(b) State the general effect of this hormone.
(c) Name the compound sprayed in orchards to release this hormone for uniform ripening.
(d) Besides ripening, give one other effect of this hormone.
questions.answer:
(a) The gaseous hormone is ETHYLENE, released by the ripe apples/fruit.
(b) Ethylene promotes and hastens the RIPENING of fruits.
(c) ETHEPHON (which releases ethylene) is sprayed to give uniform ripening.
(d) Ethylene also causes ABSCISSION (shedding) of leaves, flowers and fruits, and promotes flowering in pineapple. (Any one.)
questions.explanation: Ethylene; hastens ripening; ethephon; abscission/flowering.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A short-day plant is kept in short days and flowers normally. In another set, its long night is interrupted by a brief flash of light in the middle; these plants fail to flower.
(a) What does this experiment prove is the critical factor?
(b) Why did the light flash prevent flowering?
(c) Which pigment perceives the light?
(d) Where is the flowering stimulus perceived and where does flowering occur?
questions.answer:
(a) It proves that the continuous DARK (night) period, not the day length, is the critical factor controlling flowering.
(b) The light flash broke the long uninterrupted night; a short-day plant needs a dark period longer than a critical length, so interrupting it prevented flowering.
(c) The pigment PHYTOCHROME (Pr/Pfr) perceives the red/far-red light.
(d) The stimulus is perceived by the LEAVES, which export a signal (florigen) to the SHOOT TIPS, where flowering occurs.
questions.explanation: Dark period critical; night-break stops flowering; phytochrome; leaves perceive, shoot flowers.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Phytochrome, the photoreceptor for photoperiodism, exists in two interconvertible forms. One absorbs red light and the other absorbs far-red light, and they convert into each other on exposure to these wavelengths.
(a) Name the two forms of phytochrome.
(b) Which form absorbs red light and which absorbs far-red?
(c) Which is the biologically active form?
(d) What converts the active form back to the inactive form?
questions.answer:
(a) The two forms are Pr and Pfr.
(b) Pr absorbs RED light (about 660 nm); Pfr absorbs FAR-RED light (about 730 nm).
(c) Pfr is the biologically active form.
(d) Exposure to FAR-RED light (or a period of darkness) converts the active Pfr back to the inactive Pr.
questions.explanation: Pr and Pfr; Pr=red, Pfr=far-red; Pfr active; far-red/dark reverts it.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Winter varieties of wheat sown in spring often stay vegetative and do not flower in time. If the moist germinating seeds are first given a spell of cold near 0-5 degrees C for some weeks, the plants later flower normally and earlier.
(a) Name the process described.
(b) What environmental factor brings it about?
(c) State one benefit of the process to farmers.
(d) Which hormone can sometimes substitute for the cold requirement?
questions.answer:
(a) The process is VERNALIZATION.
(b) It is brought about by exposure to LOW TEMPERATURE (cold treatment).
(c) Benefit: it shortens the vegetative phase so the crop flowers earlier and can be harvested in the same season; winter wheat can then be sown in spring. (Any one.)
(d) GIBBERELLIN can sometimes substitute for the cold requirement.
questions.explanation: Vernalization; cold; earlier flowering/spring sowing; gibberellin substitutes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The leaflets of the sensitive plant Mimosa pudica fold up within seconds when touched, and reopen later. In contrast, a potted plant kept near a window gradually bends its shoot towards the light over a day or two.
(a) Name the type of movement shown by Mimosa and by the shoot.
(b) Which of these is directional and which is non-directional?
(c) What causes the rapid folding in Mimosa?
(d) State one way the two types of movement differ in speed and reversibility.
questions.answer:
(a) Mimosa shows a NASTIC movement (seismonasty/thigmonasty); the shoot bending to light shows a TROPIC movement (phototropism).
(b) The shoot's phototropism is DIRECTIONAL (its direction is set by the stimulus); the Mimosa response is NON-DIRECTIONAL.
(c) The rapid folding is caused by a sudden loss of TURGOR (water) in the pulvinus (swollen leaf base), not by growth.
(d) Nastic movements are usually rapid and reversible (turgor movements), whereas tropic movements are slow and permanent (growth movements).
questions.explanation: Nastic (Mimosa) vs tropic (phototropism); directional vs not; turgor loss; fast/reversible vs slow/permanent.
